The average American might sports gamble and go to Las Vegas in the hopes of striking a payday. It feels like most in my generation would prefer to protest data centers or vote for socialism, instead of trying to study and position their capital into asymmetric stocks.

Koreans on the other hand buy technology stocks in the hopes of getting rich. Betting that memory is not cyclical is by all means a WAY better trade than playing roulette or throwing up a random bet on the Chiefs versus the Eagles. 

At the same time, most Americans are invested in the market broadly and only 1/5 of people pick individual stocks, a number that has flatlined for decades. That of course means that using debt to buy stocks or trading options is much less common, which is definitely a good thing after what we are witnessing on the KOSPI.

I found the most fascinating divergence in global macro.

The most recent South Korean consumer sentiment reading sits above 100, meaning optimists outnumber pessimists, and has held near multi-year highs. 

Meanwhile U.S. consumer sentiment is at its lowest on record. 

So why does one country feel rich and the other feel broke? Both countries saw their stock markets rip to record highs this year. 

The KOSPI is up 57% compared to the S&P at just 9.5% YTD, that could explain it. But it's not necessarily the returns that create the divergence.

It's HOW citizens in each country own stocks.

Korea has 105 million active brokerage accounts in a country of 51 million people. Retail is roughly half of all trading volume. Margin debt just hit an all time high of 38.5 trillion won. Samsung and SK Hynix alone account for 51% of daily market turnover, and once you add the single stock leverage and inverse ETFs, it clears 80%.

Koreans don't have "exposure" to the market. They ARE the market. Direct, concentrated, levered. The KOSPI doubled in 9 months and every kitchen table in Seoul FELT it. That's your consumer sentiment print.

America is the opposite. 58% of families own stock but only 21% picked individual stocks, and that ownership number has been flat near 20% for three decades. The percentage of Americans trying to make multi-bagger returns is a tiny fraction of Koreans. 

Because of this, Americans have exposure to the markets but don't really feel it. They glance at a quarterly 401k statement moving up with the index and go back to paying for gas. They're not building an active trading strategy around thematics or speculating on AI bottlenecks.

Fable 5 tells me only about half of Americans might recognize Nvidia by name, even less could tell you what it does. Meanwhile, 99% of Korean people know their largest companies like Samsung and SK Hynix intimatley.

Of course, it's likely that the next consumer sentiment reading in Korea will be markedly lower after the country's stock market has fallen 20% in just the last month. Leverage, speculation, and active trading around a couple of companies is a two way street.

But certainly a fascinating difference between two economies at the center of the AI revolution.

There's a problem with memory.

I'm a memory bull and think a strong concentration is critical for any AI portfolio. But I do think the market's obsession around it is overblown compared to where we're at R/R wise with $1T market caps across the board.

What irks me about the current market is that everyone just gets fixated on one theme at a time. Right now, that's memory. If memory is down, "it's over". If memory is up, there is exuberance about the future. 

Memory stocks should not be the sentiment leader. This is a highly controversial trade and therefore it is extremely volatile and sensitive to every little piece of information, wreaking havoc on the tape.

At current PE's these co's are sitting somewhere in between being seen as a cyclical and being not. I don't see why it needs to dictate how we feel about the AI complex.

If memory really is cyclical and supply can catch up in 27-28, guess what it has NO impact on the long term potential of AI. In fact, cheaper memory is extremely bullish for the AI industry, robotics, wearables, consumer? If memory gets crushed, it's a bubble inside a bubble, other AI names that are secular will continue to scale as this technology grows in impact and TAM.

It's possible memory names can double again from here in the short/near term and get treated like structural companies in the future of tech at 15-20x PE ratios. This would be like equivalent of oil with the arrival of automobile ---> commodity producing oil companies trade at secular multiples ever since.

But is a double really that interesting? I don't think there's asymmetrical upside here worth gambling your life over for the R/R on memory at these levels. I've even heard reports of suicides in Korea after a 30% drawdown, not sure if that's true but again the set ups here with market caps at $1T just aren't worth it for extreme concentration?

Again, I'm bullish and think memory is the mother of all bottlenecks - a really important piece of every  AI portfolio and I'm long at these levels SNDK, MU etc. But the obsession around it is certainly overblown.
